text: Once you start calling real library functions like pandas's read_csv, you'll see default values, keyword arguments, and catch-all arguments everywhere. This lesson covers all three patterns, using the kind of order-processing functions you've already been writing.

A parameter can carry a default value that's used automatically when the caller skips it. calculate_total_with_tax defaults tax_rate to 0.08 -- call it with just a subtotal and you get the 8 percent rate; pass a second argument and you override it. This is exactly the shape of a call like pd.read_csv(path, sep=','), where sep already defaults to a comma.

Up to now, every argument has matched a parameter by position. Keyword arguments let you name which parameter you're setting, in any order you like. Once a function has more than one or two parameters, writing status='Cancelled' at the call site documents what that value means in a way a bare string in the third position never could.

Sometimes you don't know in advance how many values are coming. A parameter written as star args -- here, line_totals -- collects any number of extra positional arguments into a tuple. Call total_revenue with two numbers or five, and it sums whatever you hand it.

Double-star kwargs does the same job for named arguments, collecting them into a dictionary instead. build_order_record takes one required order_id, then gathers any extra named fields into extra_fields, a regular dict you can merge with .update(). This exact pattern -- a few required parameters plus kwargs for the rest -- is how pd.DataFrame and plenty of other library constructors are built.
Next, scope and returning multiple values: where a variable actually lives while your code runs, and how a function can hand back more than one answer at once.
